newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Swiss lawmakers eye protection for bank informers.
newsitem.headline: Swiss lawmakers eye protection for bank informers.

text.p: Swiss legislators want to change the law to protect the jobs of people who reveal secrets about bank accounts of Holocaust victims and Switzerland's World War Two financial role, a Sunday newspaper said.

The legal affairs committee of parliament's lower house plans to propose legislation in June after the firing of a nightwatchman who uncovered document-shredding at Switzerland's biggest bank, SonntagsZeiting said.
Committee chairwoman Lili Nabholz was not available for comment.

Several legislators have called in the past for legal protection for employees who turn over records to a commission of government-appointed historians exploring the neutral country's role as banker to both the Nazis and victims of the Holocaust.
The calls were prompted by the case of Christoph Meili, who was sacked by the security company he worked for after smuggling out documents from a shredder room at Union Bank of Switzerland (UBS).
"What happened to Meili was a scandal," legal affairs committee member Paul Rechsteiner of the Social Democrats, one of four parties in the centre-right government coalition, told SonntagsZeitung.

Meili, who said he suspected the documents from a UBS subsidiary might pertain to World War Two-era business, gave them to Zurich Jewish leaders, who alerted prosecutors to a possible violation of a ban on destroying any material that could help find unclaimed wealth.

Zurich prosecutors are investigating whether Meili should be charged for violating bank secrecy laws as well as whether the bank or its chief archivist broke the law by shredding the remaining documents Meili did not rescue.

UBS says the destruction of old records was a "regrettable accident" and insists no client records were lost that could aid the search for missing assets that Hitler's victims may have deposited in Swiss banks.
Meili, a 28-year-old father of two, has since left Switzerland for the U.S. to start a new life with his wife and children, saying he felt threatened and could not get a new job.
Meili has been hailed as a hero by Jewish leaders in Switzerland and in the United States.
